extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of sociology, journalism, and media studies; researchers interested in news selection and newsworthiness
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes Robert E. Park's 1940 sociological account of what counts as news and the implicit criteria journalists use to select news items, including talkability, sudden change, public relevance, recency, and orienting value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Talkability
rubrics_metrics.description: "News is something that will make people talk." An item with high talkability is news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Park's central criterion: if an event will generate social conversation (water-cooler talk, social-media chatter), it is newsworthy. Antipattern: facts that are important but unlikely to be discussed socially may be ignored. Related modern research: shareability/virality studies (e.g., Berger & Milkman 2012).

rubrics_metrics.name: The character of a public document
rubrics_metrics.description: News should be open, communicated, and capable of widespread circulation — possess the character of a public document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Items that are public in nature or can be disseminated widely are favored. Private/intimate matters rank lower unless they reveal broader public significance. Editors filter stories by their capacity to be publicly circulated and discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation to sudden, decisive changes
rubrics_metrics.description: News reports discrete events — sudden or decisive changes — rather than slow-developing conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Park emphasizes event-centered reporting: abrupt happenings qualify as news while gradual structural processes do not. Antipattern: treating slow trends as immediately newsworthy without a discrete 'event' or new peg. This produces a bias toward episodic coverage of events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transient and ephemeral quality (recency/perishability)
rubrics_metrics.description: News is perishable: it loses value once it ceases to be talked about; recency is intrinsic to newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recency is a necessary condition — old happenings are typically not news unless given a new hook. Editorial implication: stories must be timely or have a new angle to re-enter coverage (need a 'peg').

rubrics_metrics.name: Orienting function / orienting value
rubrics_metrics.description: News exists to orient persons and societies in the 'actual world' — it helps readers locate themselves and make sense of events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection favors items that help audiences understand their social environment. Antipattern: novelty without substantive orienting information (trivially novel items that don't help orientation) may be filtered out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: The event must matter beyond the immediate actors involved; it should have public significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories are evaluated for relevance to a broader public sphere. Private matters are deprioritized unless they reveal issues of public import. This functions as a public-vs-private filter in editorial decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continued conversation / sustained discussability
rubrics_metrics.description: News that sustains discussion across the news cycle outlives one-shot reports and is therefore more valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond initial talkability, the capacity to generate ongoing discourse (follow-ups, debate, continued sharing) increases a story's lifespan and perceived newsworthiness. Editors may prefer stories that can be developed over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversation-generation (shareability heuristic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories are judged by their ability to generate social conversation and sharing — a practical corollary to talkability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Park's notion anticipates modern metrics of shareability: selection favors items likely to be retransmitted in social networks. Editorial practices may thus privilege emotionally engaging, surprising, or conflictual items that prompt sharing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sudden-change bias (episodic over thematic coverage)
rubrics_metrics.description: A systemic bias toward covering discrete events (episodes) rather than structural conditions or thematic context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: over-coverage of isolated incidents and under-coverage of long-term trends or structural analysis. This anticipates later critiques (e.g., Iyengar's episodic/thematic asymmetry) and suggests an editorial tendency to favor spectacular events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-continuity bias / need for a new 'peg'
rubrics_metrics.description: Long-running situations are unlikely to be continuously newsworthy unless a new, discrete hook arises to make them fresh again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors often require a new angle or incident to reframe ongoing issues as news. Antipattern: assuming continuous importance makes a story stay in coverage without a fresh event or development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-vs-private filter
rubrics_metrics.description: A selection filter that privileges items exhibiting public-document qualities over private or intimate matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private issues are covered primarily when they reveal public significance (e.g., when a private scandal signals broader institutional problems). This criterion constrains what personal information becomes news.
